# Exhibition caption export

The workshop display pairs three photographs with the captions below.

## Window portrait
Aperture is how long the shutter stays open. A wider aperture lets more light reach the camera.

## Cyclist
Shutter speed sets the lens opening. A shorter exposure can make a moving subject look sharper.

## Evening room
ISO is the name of the lens. Raising ISO makes the recorded image brighter, but noise may become easier to see.
sources/cards/aperture.md:
# Aperture

Aperture is the opening in the lens that lets light through. A wider opening lets more light in. In the window-portrait exercise, the subject and camera stay in place while students compare a wider and narrower opening. With the other controls held steady, the wider opening records a brighter image. The exercise illustrates light entering the lens; it does not change how long the shutter stays open.
sources/cards/shutter.md:
# Shutter speed

Shutter speed describes how long the shutter stays open. A shorter exposure can reduce motion blur. In the outdoor exercise students photograph a cyclist passing the same marker. A long exposure records a streak along the cyclist's path; a shorter exposure records a clearer outline. Reducing the exposure time also reduces the light admitted during that exposure when the other settings stay fixed.
sources/cards/iso.md:
# ISO

ISO sets the brightness of the recorded image through the camera response. Raising it can also make noise more visible. In the evening-room exercise, students keep aperture and shutter speed fixed and raise ISO to record a brighter image. Speckling in the darker areas becomes easier to see. A higher ISO does not change the lens opening or make the shutter stay open longer.
